overview: This file documents U.S. diplomatic and intelligence monitoring of Japanese news organizations and Japanese-language newspapers in Argentina from 1940 to 1944. It traces the establishment of the Dōmei News Agency’s Buenos Aires office under Masao Tsuda; profiles the ownership, circulation, finances, and political affiliations of local Japanese newspapers; translates a wartime telephone conversation between correspondents in Buenos Aires and Tokyo; and surveys Japanese propaganda and international-news coverage during 1943. Embassy and FBI reports emphasize Argentine communications controls, the use of shortwave radio to evade cable restrictions, newsprint shortages, Japanese attitudes toward Argentina’s neutrality, and Tsuda’s collection of American press material for the Japanese government. Cross-reference sheets point to related records concerning financial support for Tsuda and Tokujiro Furuta’s connection with the Yomiuri News Agency.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1711 on the establishment of a Dōmei office in Buenos Aires
subfiles.from: Norman Armour, U.S. Ambassador to Argentina
subfiles.about: Reports Masao Tsuda’s arrival in Buenos Aires to establish the first direct local representation of the Dōmei News Agency.
subfiles.summary: Masao Tsuda arrived from New York aboard the S.S. Uruguay on December 17, intending to act as a correspondent and possibly distribute a regular Dōmei press service. Previously, the Japanese Embassy had distributed only selected Dōmei material, especially speeches by officials in Tokyo. Given Argentina’s small Japanese population and the limited importance of its two Japanese newspapers, the Embassy believed that any broader Dōmei service would probably seek to place propaganda in Argentine daily newspapers.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on payments to Masao Tsuda
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy in Argentina (Edward L. Reed), as cited
subfiles.about: Points to a separate despatch concerning payments made to Dōmei’s Buenos Aires representative Masao Tsuda.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Despatch No. 4958 of May 5, 1942, filed as 894.20235/44. Its subject is support of the Dōmei News Agency in Argentina, specifically payments made to local representative Masao Tsuda.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal on Japanese newspapers in Buenos Aires
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential information about Japanese newspapers published in Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle an enclosed memorandum based on a reliable confidential source. He notes that the same information had been made available to the American Embassy in Buenos Aires. Copies were also directed to U.S. naval and military intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: FBI memorandum profiling four Japanese newspapers
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., as enclosure
subfiles.about: Profiles the ownership, readership, circulation, political connections, and publication difficulties of four Japanese newspapers in Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes Argentin Djijo, Nighia Gjiji, Nan-A, and Nichi Nichi, giving their addresses, proprietors, circulation figures, prices, intended social constituencies, and relationships with the Japanese Embassy. It characterizes Argentin Djijo as an embassy organ and notes that Nan-A had been suspended by the embassy, while Nichi Nichi had been barred from the Argentine mails. Paper shortages and poor-quality newsprint affected all four publications.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 7746 on a Tokyo–Buenos Aires telephone conversation
subfiles.from: Edward L. Reed, Counselor of Embassy
subfiles.about: Encloses and analyzes a Japanese newspaper account of a wartime telephone conversation between correspondents in Buenos Aires and Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports a December 4 conversation between Iwashita of El Argentin Djijo and Yamauchi of the Manchuria Daily News. It warns that their discussion of American military strength, production, the Solomon Sea battle, and French North Africa might have disclosed military information, while noting that new Argentine communications controls should prevent further Japanese-language calls. Reed also highlights comments about Argentina and Chile drifting away from neutrality, Japanese government efforts to stimulate hatred of the United States and Britain, and ambiguities beneath claims of popular confidence in victory.

subfiles.title: Translation of the Tokyo–Buenos Aires telephone conversation
subfiles.about: Reproduces the reported conversation between Iwashita in Buenos Aires and Yamauchi in Tokyo about the war, neutrality, treatment of nationals, and Japanese morale.
subfiles.summary: Iwashita says Argentina and Chile preserve neutrality only in name but predicts no immediate danger to resident Japanese before a formal break with the Axis. Yamauchi claims that reports of mistreatment of Japanese nationals in America and Britain have strengthened popular anger and support for destroying those countries. He portrays Japan as prepared for a long production war, citing the slogan “If one ship is sunk we’ll build two” and public donations of scrap metal.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8500 on increased newspaper subscription rates
subfiles.from: Richard Ford, First Secretary of Embassy
subfiles.about: Reports the decision of Argentina’s three Japanese-language newspapers to raise subscription prices because of wartime newsprint shortages.
subfiles.summary: The three newspapers raised their monthly subscription rate from two to 2.50 pesos rather than reduce publication frequency or amalgamate. Ford supplies details about their page dimensions, poor paper, advertisements, staffing, and subscription-only distribution. Most international news came through Axis-based Dōmei offices and local representative Masao Tsuda, while Japanese dailies also maintained their own local correspondents.

subfiles.title: Joint subscription-rate notice by three Japanese newspapers
subfiles.from: Publishers of El Argentin Djijo, Diario Nan-A, and El Nichi-A Djidji
subfiles.about: Announces a coordinated subscription increase intended to preserve frequent publication despite the scarcity and rising cost of newsprint.
subfiles.summary: The publishers state that newsprint costs had quadrupled since the war began and that supplies were extremely difficult to obtain. They argue that reducing publication to two or three issues weekly would weaken their duty to counter fabricated reports in the enemy foreign press. The notice lists the Buenos Aires addresses and publishers of all three newspapers and raises each monthly subscription to 2.50 pesos from February 1, 1943.

subfiles.title: Report No. 10959 on Japanese coverage of international news
subfiles.from: Hugh Millard, First Secretary of Embassy
subfiles.about: Surveys the international-news themes published by Argentina’s Japanese newspapers during May and June 1943.
subfiles.summary: Millard reports that the papers relied chiefly on Spanish-language Dōmei reports retranslated into Japanese, but increasingly received Japanese-language news directly by shortwave radio to evade Argentine cable restrictions. The survey covers Japan’s “new China policy,” defenses against air raids, promises of independence for Burma and the Philippines, economic mobilization, the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, Yamamoto’s death, occupation policies, the Shanghai Jewish ghetto, and military developments across Asia and the Pacific. It also records claims concerning hospital ships, action against foreign currency, Taiwanese naval recruiting, a Buddhist conference, and Japanese anxieties about Argentina’s revolution and a possible break with the Axis. Reports of strikes and political discord in the United States were welcomed in Tokyo as evidence that internal division might assist Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Tokujiro Furuta and the Yomiuri News Agency
subfiles.from: Department of Justice (J. Edgar Hoover), as cited
subfiles.about: Points to a Justice Department letter concerning Tokujiro Furuta’s connection with the Yomiuri News Agency in Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers researchers to a May 1, 1944 letter from the Department of Justice and Hoover. The original, filed as 894.20235/172, contains information about Tokujiro Furuta and the Yomiuri News Agency’s Buenos Aires operation.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Masao Tsuda’s collection of American press material
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports that Masao Tsuda was sending extracts from selected American newspapers and magazines to the Japanese government for propaganda purposes.
subfiles.summary: According to a confidential source, Tsuda had instructions to transmit material from Time, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and the New Republic because copies reached Tokyo only after delays, often through Russia and India. A cable sent shortly after publication of the “United States White Book” demanded an urgent five-hundred-word summary of its treatment of Japan. The FBI concluded that Tsuda supplied material for Japanese propaganda; the OCR date is garbled, but the receipt stamp and the following reply identify the letter as February 9, 1943.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning the Tsuda report
subfiles.from: George A. Gordon, Acting Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Coordination
subfiles.to: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the FBI’s information about Masao Tsuda and recommends sharing it with the Office of Censorship.
subfiles.summary: Gordon thanks Hoover for the February 9 report concerning Masao Tsuda and says that it is of interest to the State Department. He suggests that the FBI also transmit the information to the Office of Censorship because Tsuda’s activities fall within that office’s responsibilities.

interest: The file is especially useful for its unusually detailed evidence about the small Japanese-language press in wartime Argentina, including circulation figures, addresses, staffing, prices, paper quality, political alignments, and relationships with the Japanese Embassy. The translated telephone conversation and the reports on cable controls and shortwave reception reveal how news moved between Tokyo and Buenos Aires and how correspondents adapted to censorship. The documents also show the overlap between journalism, propaganda, diaspora politics, and intelligence collection, while the Embassy’s sometimes speculative and hostile language provides evidence of U.S. wartime perceptions as well as of Japanese activity. The cross-reference sheets demonstrate how relevant intelligence was dispersed across the State Department’s decimal filing system and identify related records that may preserve additional financial and personnel information.
